title: The triad, and the leg that fails quietly
intro: Four steps from 'these things are related' to 'this system can be reversed'.

steps.title: A relation earns the name
steps.body: Reflexive, symmetric, transitive — pass all three and the relation **partitions** the set into disjoint classes. That partition is the whole payoff: you stop reasoning about individual parts and start reasoning about groups. Build the 0/1 adjacency matrix and each leg becomes a matrix test: diagonal all ones, `M == Mᵀ`, and wherever two-step reach exists there is already a direct edge.

points.label: Reflexive
points.note: Diagonal all 1s. Almost free — most engineering relations are reflexive by definition ('shares a subnet with' includes itself).

points.label: Symmetric
points.note: M equals its transpose. Also usually free: physical relations rarely point one way.

points.label: Transitive
points.note: The expensive one. It asserts something about pairs you never measured — which is exactly why it is the leg that fails.

steps.title: The PCB that wasn't an equivalence
steps.body: Continuity probing says pin 1 connects to pin 4, and pin 4 connects to pin 9. Both readings are true. Every pin connects to itself, and the relation is symmetric. But nobody closed **pin 1 ~ pin 9**, so transitivity fails and 'shares a 0-ohm pathway' does not partition the board. The net list built from it is wrong — and nothing in the data looks wrong.

steps.title: Functions fail in two different ways
steps.body: Read `f: A → B` as a matrix with rows = codomain, columns = domain. **Injective** = at most one 1 per row; break it and two keys drive one register — ghosting, and the input is unrecoverable. **Surjective** = at least one 1 per row; break it and a service sits deployed with no route reaching it — dead code. One failure destroys information, the other wastes capacity. They are not variations of the same bug.

steps.title: Composition inherits the weakest stage
steps.body: `(g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x))` exists only when Range(f) ⊆ Domain(g). Chain two bijections and the composite inverts exactly — decrypt ∘ deserialize returns the original payload. Put one saturating stage in the chain and it is over: past its stop, a hydraulic ram maps **every** larger stick angle to the same 10° of deflection. The preimage of 10° stops being a value and becomes a set.

points.label: Monotonic chain
points.note: Strictly increasing throughout: every horizontal line meets the curve once. Invertible, and the inverse is computable in closed form.

points.label: Saturating chain
points.note: Flat past the ram's stop. The line δ = 10° meets the curve infinitely often — telemetry in that region cannot be reconstructed by anyone, ever.

recap: Transitivity is the leg that fails, and it fails silently because it is a claim about unmeasured pairs. Injectivity failure loses information; surjectivity failure wastes capacity. A composite chain is invertible only if it stays a bijection end to end — so the design question is always 'which stage could go many-to-one?'
